stories.headline: S&P 500 SHEDS 2.00% TO 7,176, NASDAQ 100 DROPS 2.18% TO 26,517 AS RISK-OFF TONE DEEPENS
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 2.00% to 7,176 and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 2.18% to 26,517, extending the index's multi-week slide as traders priced in firmer Fed hawkishness, leadership turmoil at Nvidia, and a volatile debut from the year's largest tech IPO all on the same session.
stories.explain: A broad decline across both a value-tilted benchmark like the S&P 500 and a tech-heavy one like the Nasdaq 100 signals a market-wide repricing of discount rates and risk appetite rather than a single-sector story, since idiosyncratic news in one name can't move either index by two full percentage points on its own. With fed funds futures now leaning toward a December hike rather than a cut, higher expected real rates mechanically lower the present value of long-duration growth stocks' future cash flows, which is why the sell-off hit richly-valued AI-linked names hardest.

stories.headline: ANTHROPIC'S ANT POPS 34% AT THE OPEN, THEN FADES TO CLOSE UP 17% IN LARGEST AI IPO ON RECORD
stories.body: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion, then opened trading on the Nasdaq at $111.50 — up 34% — before giving back most of the gain to close its first session at $97.17, up 17.07%, valuing the company near $1.25 trillion.
stories.explain: The 34% gap between the $83 offer price and the $111.50 opening trade is the first-day 'IPO pop,' the premium underwriters build in by pricing below their own estimate of fair value to guarantee allocated institutional buyers an immediate profit and ensure the deal doesn't fail to clear. The fade from $111.50 to a $97.17 close shows those early buyers taking profit once the stock became freely tradable, a pattern known as flipping, which is also why a strong open is a weak predictor of where a new listing settles once real two-sided price discovery takes over.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS RISE TO 77% AS TRADERS AWAIT OCT. PCE NOV. 25, NOVEMBER JOBS DEC. 4
stories.body: Futures-implied odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting climbed to roughly 77%, up from 28% in mid-August, with the fed funds rate still at 3.75%-4.00% following October's hold; the Oct. core PCE report on Nov. 25 and the November jobs report on Dec. 4 are the last two data points before the decision.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures embed a probability-weighted average of possible rate paths, so the climb from 28% to 77% in three months reflects a string of data — not one release — convincing traders that inflation has proven stickier than the market assumed when cut odds still dominated. Because both the core PCE and jobs reports land in the eight days before the meeting, each has the mechanical power to swing that 77% figure sharply in either direction, which is exactly why equity and bond desks are positioning defensively into both prints rather than waiting for the FOMC itself.

stories.headline: HUANG'S CONGRESSIONAL TESTIMONY SET FOR DEC. 1, NVIDIA GENERAL COUNSEL TETER TO FOLLOW DEC. 2
stories.body: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Nov. 12 after disclosures about a relationship with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects of ties to Chinese espionage, is now scheduled for a closed-door transcribed interview before House committees on Dec. 1, with Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter following Dec. 2; interim CEO Colette Kress continues running the company as the board searches for a permanent successor.
stories.explain: A transcribed interview, unlike a public hearing, is negotiated privately between committee staff and counsel and carries no subpoena deadline, which is why the date has already slipped twice since mid-November. For Nvidia shareholders, the overhang is less about the testimony's content and more about duration of uncertainty at the top of a company whose stock trades heavily on confidence in its product roadmap and export-control posture, with no permanent CEO named and the national-security angle still unresolved.

stories.headline: GOLD SINKS 2.59% TO ~$3,628 ON FIRMER RATE PATH AS WTI CRUDE ADDS 1.14% TO ~$83
stories.body: Gold fell 2.59% to roughly $3,628 an ounce, extending its slide from a one-year high near $3,880 earlier this month, as rising December hike odds lifted real yields and dulled the appeal of a non-yielding asset, while WTI crude rose 1.14% to about $83 a barrel.
stories.explain: Gold pays no coupon or dividend, so its opportunity cost rises in lockstep with real yields; when Fed hike odds jump from 28% to 77% over a few months, the implied real rate path steepens and institutional gold holdings become more expensive to carry, which is the direct mechanism behind today's drop. Oil's smaller, opposite move reflects a separate driver — supply and geopolitical risk pricing rather than the discount-rate channel — which is why the two 'inflation hedge' commodities aren't moving together today.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX STEADY AT 103.93 AS TREASURY YIELD HOLDS NEAR 5.05% HEADING INTO KEY DATA WEEK
stories.body: The DXY dollar index was roughly flat at 103.93 (+0.02%) and the 10-year Treasury yield held near 5.05%, both consolidating just below multi-month highs as traders position ahead of next week's core PCE print, the last major inflation read before the Fed's December decision.
stories.explain: A dollar index and long-end yield that are both holding near cycle highs without further upside is often a sign the hawkish repricing has largely run its course for now, with the market waiting for confirming data rather than pushing positioning further on sentiment alone. Because the 10-year yield reflects expected short-term rates plus a term premium, its stall near 5.05% even as equities sold off 2% suggests today's stock move was driven more by risk-premium repricing in equities specifically than by a fresh leg up in the broader rate outlook.

watchlist: Oct. core PCE inflation data — Nov. 25, the last major print before the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting
November jobs report — Dec. 4, landing four days before the FOMC decision
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds near 77% with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%
Jensen Huang's closed-door House testimony — Dec. 1, with Nvidia GC Tim Teter following Dec. 2
ANT's post-IPO trading — closed first session at $97.17 (+17% from offer); index-inclusion speculation building

deepDive.title: Why Anthropic's IPO Popped 34% at the Open and Still Faded to 17%
content: Today's biggest market story wasn't just that Anthropic went public — it's the shape of the move. ANT priced at $83 a share, opened at $111.50, and closed at $97.17. That 34%-then-17% pattern is not random noise; it's the signature of how IPO pricing actually works, and it shows up in nearly every hot offering, from Airbnb's 2020 debut to SpaceX's recent record-setting listing. Understanding why underwriters leave that much money on the table — and why the market claws some of it back within hours — is one of the clearest windows into how primary and secondary markets price the same share differently.

The mechanism starts with book-building. Underwriters survey institutional demand before the deal prices, then deliberately set the offer price below their own estimate of where the stock will trade once public — academics call this 'IPO underpricing.' It exists for a practical reason: allocated buyers (the banks' best clients) need a near-certain profit to keep participating in future deals, and a price that's too aggressive risks a deal failing to clear entirely. For a $1.3 trillion-plus valuation company with $26 billion in strategic commitments from chipmakers and cloud providers, as Anthropic had, the bank's incentive to avoid a failed or flat debut is enormous — so they leave room to pop.

What's less obvious is why the pop fades. The investors who got $83 allocations have an immediate, nearly risk-free gain once the stock opens at $111.50, and many sell into that strength within the first session — a behavior the Street calls 'flipping.' That selling pressure meets a public market that hasn't yet done its own independent valuation work; retail and late-arriving institutional demand that chased the open absorbs the flip-driven supply, and the price settles lower. This is exactly the pattern seen in 2021's hottest SPAC and tech debuts, where some first-day pops exceeding 100% were cut by more than half within the first week once allocation-driven buying was exhausted.

For a market already repricing Fed hike odds and digesting Nvidia's leadership vacancy, ANT's fade matters beyond one stock. A close at 17% above offer — strong, but a third of the opening move — tells you real secondary-market demand for a $1.2+ trillion AI bet is genuine but not unlimited, especially with the 10-year yield near 5.05% raising the discount rate applied to any long-duration growth story. Watch whether ANT holds above $97 into next week; a further slide toward the IPO price would suggest the index-inclusion and strategic-investor narrative isn't enough to offset a market broadly repricing for higher-for-longer rates.
